text.en: Alexander II signed the manifesto freeing the serfs on 3 March 1861 (19 February Old Style); the very next day Lincoln became US president.
China's Taiping Rebellion (1850–1864) overlapped with the American Civil War and cost an estimated 20–30 million lives — many times more.
1869: in March Mendeleev presented his periodic table, and in November the Suez Canal opened.
The last quagga died at Amsterdam Zoo on 12 August 1883 — two weeks before Krakatoa's catastrophic eruption.
Only 37 years after the Meiji Restoration, when Japan was just leaving its samurai order behind, it defeated Russia in the war of 1904–1905.
The Eiffel Tower opened in spring 1889, and in June van Gogh painted The Starry Night at the Saint-Rémy asylum. He himself thought it a failure.
1861: Russia abolished serfdom, and a united Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed in Turin.
Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859) and Mendeleev's periodic law (1869) are just ten years apart.
In 1895 Popov demonstrated a radio receiver in St Petersburg, and the Lumière brothers held the first paid film screening in Paris.
1908: the Tunguska blast flattened 2,000 km² of Siberian forest, and the Messina earthquake killed some 80,000 people.
Russia abolished serfdom in 1861 and the USA slavery in 1865; Brazil was the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery, only in 1888.
Bell wanted people to answer the telephone with a sailor's 'Ahoy!'. What stuck was 'Hello!', suggested by Thomas Edison in 1877.
The telephone and the end of samurai swords arrived together: Bell patented the telephone in March 1876, and on 28 March Japan banned carrying swords in public.
In Japan, 1872 ended on the 2nd of December. Switching to the Gregorian calendar, the Meiji government declared that the next day would be 1 January 1873.
When the Americans 'opened' Japan, they gave it a toy train. In 1854 a miniature steam locomotive and a telegraph set were shown off as marvels of Western technology, to great acclaim.
Nintendo is as old as the Eiffel Tower: it was founded in Kyoto on 23 September 1889 to make hanafuda playing cards, the same year the tower opened.
Samurai and cowboys were contemporaries: the samurai's last stand at Shiroyama came in September 1877, the Gunfight at the O.K. Corral just four years later, in 1881.
Everest was named after a man who objected. George Everest, former head of the survey of India, argued his name could not be written in Hindi or pronounced by locals. It was adopted anyway in 1865.
The King of Siam offered America elephants. Mongkut's 1861 letter reached Lincoln, who politely declined: the climate was unsuitable, he wrote, and steam engines already did the hauling.
The first transatlantic telegram took 16 hours to send: Queen Victoria's 98-word greeting to the US president in 1858. The cable itself lasted about three weeks.
English owes the word 'jumbo' to an elephant. Jumbo was the star of London Zoo until P. T. Barnum bought him in 1882, and his name gave us jumbo jets and jumbo shrimp.
The Brooklyn Bridge was proven safe with elephants: in May 1884 P. T. Barnum marched 21 of them across, led by the famous Jumbo, easing public doubts and advertising his circus at once.
The Ferris wheel was America's answer to the Eiffel Tower. George Ferris's 80-metre wheel was the star of the 1893 Chicago fair, four years after the one in Paris.
The Statue of Liberty was a shiny reddish brown, like a new penny. It turned green within about twenty years of its 1886 dedication, and that patina now protects it from corrosion.

The American Civil War began in Wilmer McLean's yard and ended in his parlour. The First Battle of Bull Run was fought on his farm in 1861; he moved to quiet Appomattox, and in 1865 Lee surrendered in his house.
The US paid a Civil War pension until 2020. Irene Triplett, daughter of a veteran who fought first for the Confederacy and then for the Union, received $73.13 a month.
Slaves in Texas learned they were free 900 days late: Lincoln's proclamation took effect on 1 January 1863, but it was announced in Galveston only on 19 June 1865, now celebrated as Juneteenth.

The oldest recording of a human voice was made in 1860 but first heard in 2008. Scott de Martinville's phonautograph traced sound on sooty paper and could not play it back at all; computers finally did.
Jeans were patented in 1873, or rather the copper rivets on work trousers. Tailor Jacob Davis came up with riveting the pockets and shared the patent with his cloth supplier, Levi Strauss.
'I have seen my death!' cried Röntgen's wife when she saw the first X-ray of her hand about six weeks after he discovered the rays.

Alfred Nobel read his own obituary eight years before he died. When his brother Ludvig died in 1888, a French paper wrote him off instead; by a popular account, this pushed him to leave his fortune to the prizes.
The first car to break 100 km/h was electric: in 1899 Belgian driver Camille Jenatzy hit almost 106 km/h near Paris in the torpedo-shaped La Jamais Contente, 'The Never Satisfied'.
Under an 1865 British law, a man with a red flag had to walk 60 yards ahead of any road locomotive. The Red Flag Act capped speed at 2 mph in towns and 4 mph in the country.
The Wright brothers' first flight was shorter than a Boeing 747's wingspan: Orville covered 37 metres, while the first jumbo jet's wings spanned about 60.
The pneumatic tyre was invented by a vet for his son's tricycle. John Boyd Dunlop made it in 1887, only to learn that Robert Thomson had patented the idea back in 1846.

The founder of the Red Cross won the first Nobel Peace Prize while living in a care home. Henry Dunant went bankrupt in 1867 and lived in obscurity for decades until a journalist found him in Heiden, Switzerland.
There were no gold medals at the first modern Olympics in 1896. Winners got silver and an olive branch, runners-up copper, and third place got nothing.
The 1900 Paris Olympics dragged on for over five months, from 14 May to 28 October. They were the only Games with live pigeon shooting and the first with women competitors.
The first official international football match ended 0–0: Scotland and England played it in Glasgow on 30 November 1872 before 4,000 spectators.
Reporter Nellie Bly went round the world in 72 days, beating Jules Verne's Phileas Fogg. On the way she visited Verne himself in Amiens; within months her record fell to 67 days.
Queen Victoria went to Buffalo Bill's Wild West show. In her Golden Jubilee year of 1887, the cowboys and Native performers gave over 300 shows in London and sold more than 2.5 million tickets.

Tolkien was born in South Africa, in Bloemfontein, in 1892. As a child he was bitten there by a large baboon spider, though he did not remember it; the family left for England when he was about three.

Painters of the 18th and 19th centuries used paint made from mummies. 'Mummy brown' was ground from Egyptian mummies; on learning this in 1881, the Pre-Raphaelite Edward Burne-Jones gave his tube a solemn burial.
Aida was not written for the opening of the Suez Canal. The Khedive asked Verdi for an opera for the celebrations and he refused; Aida came later, premiering in Cairo on 24 December 1871.
Audiences did not flee the Lumières' Arrival of a Train; it is most likely an urban legend. Historians have found no contemporary report of a panic, which would surely have made the papers.
Méliès's 1902 A Trip to the Moon was a smash hit and a piracy victim. Copies were duplicated in the US, Edison's people among them, and Méliès never saw most of the profits.
The biggest gold nugget ever found lay just 3 cm below the surface. The Welcome Stranger, with 72 kg of pure gold, was dug up by two Cornish miners in Victoria on 5 February 1869.
Canberra exists because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would let the other be capital. The compromise city was designed by Americans Walter and Marion Griffin and named in 1913.
Welsh is still spoken in Argentine Patagonia. In 1865 the clipper Mimosa landed 153 settlers from Wales; today Chubut province has between 1,500 and 5,000 Welsh speakers, by various estimates.
In 1864 Spain seized Peru's bird-dropping islands. Guano from the Chincha Islands brought in almost 60% of Peru's government revenue, and the seizure led to war between Spain, Peru and Chile.
Under an 1856 law a US citizen can claim any unclaimed island for America, provided it is covered in bird droppings. The Guano Islands Act was written for fertiliser and is still on the books.

Persia's Naser al-Din Shah was one of Iran's first photographers. He set up a studio in the Golestan Palace and was photographed hundreds of times, and in 1873 he became the first modern Iranian monarch to visit Europe, keeping a travel diary.
The owner of Neuschwanstein, the castle that inspired Disney, lived there for just 172 days. Ludwig II began it in 1869, and within six weeks of his death in 1886 it was opened to paying visitors.
Two lions brought a British railway in Kenya to a halt. In 1898 work on the Tsavo bridge stopped and Prime Minister Salisbury spoke of the man-eaters in Parliament. The death toll is still disputed.
P. T. Barnum exhibited a fake of a fake. In 1869 a 3-metre gypsum 'petrified giant' was 'dug up' in New York State; refused the chance to buy it, Barnum made a copy and declared the original a fraud.

Olivier salad was invented in the 1860s by Lucien Olivier, a chef of French and Belgian origin at Moscow's Hermitage restaurant. One of the first printed recipes, from 1894, called for hazel grouse, crayfish tails, capers and olives.
Alaska cost the United States about 2 cents an acre: $7.2 million for some 1.5 million km². Critics of the deal called it 'Seward's Folly' and 'Seward's Icebox'.

Mendeleev corrected the discoverer of an element he had never seen. Lecoq de Boisbaudran found gallium in 1875 and measured its density at 4.7 g/cm³. Mendeleev wrote to tell him to measure again — and was right.
Tchaikovsky helped open Carnegie Hall. At the New York hall's first concert on 5 May 1891 he conducted alongside Walter Damrosch, and found the auditorium 'unusually impressive and grand'.
The matryoshka is younger than the Eiffel Tower. The tower opened in 1889, the first nesting doll was made in the 1890s — and it too found fame in Paris, winning a medal at the 1900 World's Fair.
Tsiolkovsky published his rocket equation in 1903 — the year the Wright brothers first flew. Deaf from the age of nine, he was self-taught and spent his life as a provincial schoolteacher.
The first Russian Nobel laureate was the physiologist Ivan Pavlov in 1904 — honoured not for his famous conditioned reflexes but for his work on digestion.
Kandinsky took up painting at 30. In 1896 he gave up a promising career teaching law and economics and moved to Munich; some fifteen years later he was among the creators of abstract art.

Leo Tolstoy corresponded with Gandhi. Their letters lasted only a year, until Tolstoy's death in 1910, but Gandhi named his South African community Tolstoy Farm and called Tolstoy the greatest apostle of non-violence.
Just ten years after the Wright brothers' first flight, a plane with a toilet took off. Sikorsky's four-engined Ilya Muromets of 1913 also had a heated cabin, a bedroom and electric light.

The Bolsheviks took their name from the 'majority' at the 1903 party congress — even though on the key dispute, who counted as a party member, Martov's supporters, the future Mensheviks, won the vote.
In 1867 the map of North America changed twice: in March Russia sold Alaska to the United States, and on 1 July Canada came into being next door.

Phileas Fogg's race was made possible by 1869. In May the US transcontinental railroad was completed, in November the Suez Canal opened, and three years later Jules Verne sent his hero round the world in 80 days.

On the very day Custer died at the Little Bighorn, Bell was showing off the telephone. On 25 June 1876 Brazil's Emperor Pedro II tried it at the Philadelphia Centennial, while in Montana the Lakota and Cheyenne routed the cavalry.
Five weeks after Ethiopia routed an Italian army at Adwa, the first modern Olympics opened in Athens. The victory of 1 March 1896 kept Ethiopia independent through the Scramble for Africa.
A Crimean War officer lived to be filmed. Leo Tolstoy served in besieged Sevastopol in 1854–55, and in 1908, around his 80th birthday, he was caught on film — the footage survives.
People reached the South Pole before the Titanic sank. Amundsen planted his flag there on 14 December 1911; the liner went down four months later, in April 1912.

Around 1890 nearly 20 tonnes of mummified cats were shipped to England as fertiliser. They came from a vast cat cemetery near Beni Hasan in Egypt: tens of thousands of sacred animals ended up on fields.
Under US law the tomato is a vegetable. Botanists call it a berry, but in 1893 the Supreme Court ruled that since tomatoes are served with dinner, not as dessert, they must be taxed as vegetables.
Big Ben is still regulated with old pennies. Placing one on the pendulum shifts its centre of mass slightly, and the clock gains about 0.4 seconds a day.

On Yap, money takes the form of stone discs up to 3.6 m across. They are not moved; only ownership changes. One sank in transit, yet it kept being used for payment: everyone knew it was there on the seabed.

The Irish captain David O’Keefe got rich as a money carrier, for stone money. He shipped huge discs from Palau to Yap, took payment in copra and became known as “King of Yap”; Hollywood later made a film about him.

The legendary Pony Express lasted only 18 months. Riders carried mail halfway across America in 10 days, but in October 1861 the telegraph linked the coasts, and two days later the company announced it would close.

In besieged Paris in 1870, letters were photographed onto microfilm so a single pigeon could carry thousands at once. Dispatches came back by pigeon too, and were projected onto a wall to be copied out.

The only casualty of the Pig War between the US and Britain was a pig. The border dispute that began with a farmer’s shot in 1859 dragged on for 13 years and was settled by an arbitrator: the German Kaiser.
Tea bags, the popular story goes, were an accident. In 1908 the New York merchant Thomas Sullivan sent out samples in silk pouches, and customers brewed them without unpacking.
Margarine was invented for a prize offered by Napoleon III. The emperor wanted cheap butter for the army and the poor, and in 1869 the chemist Mège-Mouriès won with oleomargarine made from beef fat.

The greatest find from the Antikythera wreck went unnoticed at first. Bronze statues came up in 1901, but only in 1902 did archaeologist Valerios Stais spot a gear wheel in a dull lump of corroded metal.

For 130 years the kilogram was not a formula but an object. A platinum-iridium cylinder from 1889, kept under three glass bells in a vault near Paris, set the world's weights until 2019, when the kilogram was redefined via Planck's constant.

A German hygienist drank a cholera culture to prove Koch wrong. In 1892 Max von Pettenkofer swallowed a broth teeming with cholera bacteria and got away with a mild upset. Koch was right all the same.

Peru's Day of Medicine honours a student who infected himself for science. In 1885 Daniel Alcides Carrión inoculated himself with blood from a patient's wart and proved it was the same disease as Oroya fever. It killed him, and now bears his name.

Purple went from emperors to London fashion thanks to a student's failed experiment. For centuries the dye came from thousands of sea snails; then Perkin, trying to make quinine, got one from coal tar.

Saccharin was discovered by not washing up before dinner. In 1879 chemist Constantin Fahlberg noticed his bread tasted sweet, and traced it to a compound from his Johns Hopkins lab still on his fingers.

In 1859 telegraph operators sent messages without batteries; space supplied the power. A solar storm induced current in the wires, and operators between Boston and Portland disconnected their batteries and worked that way for about two hours.
In 1859 the aurora was so bright that gold miners in the Rocky Mountains woke in the night and began making breakfast, thinking it was morning. The lights were seen as far south as Cuba and Hawaii.

The founding work of genetics went unnoticed for 34 years. Mendel published his laws in 1866 in a provincial natural history journal, and the world learned of them only in 1900, when three botanists rediscovered them almost at once.

The father of genetics failed his exam to become a science teacher, more than once. Mendel flunked it in 1850 and failed the oral again in 1856. He kept teaching without the certificate, starting his pea experiments in those same years.

An Arizona observatory was built to study Martian canals. Millionaire Percival Lowell founded it in 1894 to observe the Martian civilisation. There were no canals, but in 1930 the observatory discovered Pluto.

In 1904 a physicist debunked a discovery by slipping part of the apparatus into his pocket. Robert Wood quietly removed the prism from Blondlot's set-up, and Blondlot went on 'seeing' N-rays. Hundreds of papers on them had already appeared.

Röntgen refused to patent his rays and gave his Nobel Prize money, from the first physics prize ever, to his university. He believed discoveries belonged to everyone and did not even want the rays named after him.

Marie Curie's notebooks are still radioactive. They are kept in lead-lined boxes at the National Library of France, and readers must sign a waiver and wear protective gear. Radium-226 takes 1,600 years to lose half its activity.

Marie Curie is the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences: physics in 1903 and chemistry in 1911. Her daughter Irène won one too, and the Curie family collected five Nobel Prizes in all.

Pain relief in childbirth became respectable thanks to a queen. In 1853 Victoria gave birth to Prince Leopold under chloroform, called it 'blessed', and arguments over whether easing labour pains was sinful soon faded.

In 1910 people bought 'comet pills'. Astronomers had found poisonous cyanogen in Halley's Comet's tail, which Earth was due to pass through, and hucksters sold pills and gas masks. The gas was far too thin to do any harm.

The telephone was invented twice on the same day. On 14 February 1876 both Alexander Graham Bell and Elisha Gray filed papers for similar devices at the patent office, and who came first was fought over in court for years.
Heroin was once sold as a cough medicine. In 1898 Bayer marketed it as a safe substitute for morphine; it had been made by the same chemist, and within days of, aspirin.

Coca-Cola was invented by a pharmacist as a medicine. In 1886 Atlanta druggist John Pemberton sold his syrup as a remedy for headaches and fatigue, at five cents a glass from a pharmacy soda fountain.

In 1897 the state of Indiana nearly passed a law on the value of pi. The House voted unanimously for a bill implying pi = 3.2; it was halted in the Senate because a mathematics professor happened to be in town.
The safety lift was sold with a stunt. At a New York exhibition in 1854 Elisha Otis rode a platform up and had the rope cut. It jolted and held, and Otis announced: 'All safe, gentlemen, all safe!'

Max Planck was told not to study physics because almost everything had already been discovered. Professor Philipp von Jolly said so in 1874. Twenty-six years later Planck launched quantum theory, and physics was never the same.

The head of the US Patent Office never said 'everything that can be invented has been invented'. The line is pinned on Charles Duell in 1899, but there is no evidence for it, and his reports in fact looked forward to new inventions.

Edison did not invent the light bulb: about twenty inventors made incandescent lamps before him, including Russia's Alexander Lodygin, patented in 1874. Edison's feat was a long-lasting bulb and a whole power system.
Wittgenstein and Hitler were born six days apart and went to the same school. Both were born in April 1889 and around 1904 attended the Realschule in Linz, though in different years.
Nietzsche became a professor at 24, before he even had a doctorate. Basel offered him the chair of classical philology in 1869, and Leipzig then granted him the degree without a dissertation.
